items.stem: Which term is defined as "a flattened membrane sac inside a chloroplast containing photosystems, electron carriers and ATP synthase"?
items.answer: Thylakoid
items.markingKey: Thylakoid: a flattened membrane sac inside a chloroplast containing photosystems, electron carriers and ATP synthase.

items.stem: Explain why photosynthesis is described as an energy transfer process.
items.answer: Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll and transferred to chemical energy in ATP and reduced NADP, and then to chemical energy in carbohydrates such as triose phosphate.
items.markingKey: light energy absorbed [1]; to ATP / reduced NADP [1]; to carbohydrate [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain the difference between an absorption spectrum and an action spectrum, and why the two are similar in shape.
items.answer: Absorption: light absorbed by a pigment at each wavelength; action: rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength; similar because the light absorbed by the pigments is what drives photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: absorption defined [1]; action defined [1]; absorbed light used in photosynthesis [1] [3]

items.stem: Arjun separated the pigments in a leaf extract by thin-layer chromatography. The solvent front moved 10.9 cm. Three spots were seen: spot A (orange-yellow) 10.2 cm, spot B (grey) 8.6 cm, spot C (blue-green) 7.3 cm from the origin. Published Rf values for this solvent are: carotene: 0.95; phaeophytin: 0.81; xanthophyll: 0.71; chlorophyll a: 0.65; chlorophyll b: 0.45. Calculate the Rf value of each spot.
items.markingKey: distance ÷ solvent front [1]; all three correct [1] [2]

items.stem: Ravi separated the pigments in a leaf extract by thin-layer chromatography. The solvent front moved 11.9 cm. Three spots were seen: spot A (orange-yellow) 11.5 cm, spot B (grey) 9.9 cm, spot C (yellow-green) 5.2 cm from the origin. Published Rf values for this solvent are: carotene: 0.95; phaeophytin: 0.81; xanthophyll: 0.71; chlorophyll a: 0.65; chlorophyll b: 0.45. (a) Use the Rf values to identify the pigments. (b) Suggest why thin-layer chromatography gives better separation than paper chromatography.
items.answer: (a) A = carotene; B = phaeophytin; C = chlorophyll b (b) The finer, more uniform stationary phase gives faster runs and sharper, more compact spots.
items.markingKey: (a) two correct [1]; all three [1] [2] (b) The finer, more uniform stationary phase gives faster runs and sharper, more compact spots [1]

items.stem: Researchers in Manila measured the action spectrum of a cyanobacterium. Unlike a typical land plant, its rate of photosynthesis was high at 520 nm, a wavelength that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly. (a) Explain why this is an advantage for the organism in its habitat. (b) Explain how the structure of the chloroplast allows the light-dependent and light-independent reactions to take place at the same time.
items.answer: (a) Red and blue light are absorbed by water (or by the canopy), so the light reaching it is mainly green/blue-green; pigments that absorb these wavelengths allow photosynthesis. (b) Light-dependent reactions on thylakoid membranes and Calvin cycle enzymes in the stroma are separate compartments, close together, so ATP and reduced NADP pass directly to the stroma.
items.markingKey: (a) light quality in habitat [1]; can use available wavelengths [1] [2] (b) separate locations [1]; products pass directly to stroma [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a mixture of pigments is more advantageous to a plant than chlorophyll a alone.
items.answer: Different pigments absorb different wavelengths, so a wider range of the light spectrum is used and passed to the reaction centre, increasing the rate of photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: different wavelengths absorbed [1]; energy passed to reaction centre / more light used [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how chromatography separates photosynthetic pigments.
items.answer: Pigments differ in solubility in the solvent and in attraction to the paper/stationary phase; more soluble, less strongly adsorbed pigments travel further with the solvent, so pigments form separate spots.
items.markingKey: solubility in solvent [1]; adsorption to stationary phase [1]; different distances [1] [3]

items.stem: Diego separated the pigments in a leaf extract by thin-layer chromatography. The solvent front moved 9.3 cm. Three spots were seen: spot A (orange-yellow) 8.9 cm, spot B (blue-green) 5.9 cm, spot C (yellow-green) 4 cm from the origin. Published Rf values for this solvent are: carotene: 0.95; phaeophytin: 0.81; xanthophyll: 0.71; chlorophyll a: 0.65; chlorophyll b: 0.45. Use the Rf values to identify the pigments.
items.answer: A = carotene; B = chlorophyll a; C = chlorophyll b
items.markingKey: two correct [1]; all three [1] [2]

items.stem: Hana separated the pigments in a leaf extract by thin-layer chromatography. The solvent front moved 10.7 cm. Three spots were seen: spot A (grey) 8.9 cm, spot B (yellow) 7.5 cm, spot C (blue-green) 6.6 cm from the origin. Published Rf values for this solvent are: carotene: 0.95; phaeophytin: 0.81; xanthophyll: 0.71; chlorophyll a: 0.65; chlorophyll b: 0.45. (a) Use the Rf values to identify the pigments. (b) Suggest why thin-layer chromatography gives better separation than paper chromatography.
items.answer: (a) A = phaeophytin; B = xanthophyll; C = chlorophyll a (b) The finer, more uniform stationary phase gives faster runs and sharper, more compact spots.
items.markingKey: (a) two correct [1]; all three [1] [2] (b) The finer, more uniform stationary phase gives faster runs and sharper, more compact spots [1]

items.stem: Researchers in Bangkok measured the action spectrum of a cyanobacterium. Unlike a typical land plant, its rate of photosynthesis was high at 540 nm, a wavelength that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly. (a) Suggest an explanation for the high rate of photosynthesis at this wavelength. (b) Explain how the structure of the chloroplast allows the light-dependent and light-independent reactions to take place at the same time.
items.answer: (a) The organism has accessory pigments (e.g. phycoerythrin / fucoxanthin) that absorb light at about 540 nm and pass the energy to chlorophyll a in the reaction centre. (b) Light-dependent reactions on thylakoid membranes and Calvin cycle enzymes in the stroma are separate compartments, close together, so ATP and reduced NADP pass directly to the stroma.
items.markingKey: (a) accessory pigment [1]; absorbs this wavelength [1]; energy passed to reaction centre [1] [3] (b) separate locations [1]; products pass directly to stroma [1] [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the flow of electrons from PSI back to the electron transport chain and back to PSI, producing ATP only"?
items.answer: Cyclic photophosphorylation
items.markingKey: Cyclic photophosphorylation: the flow of electrons from PSI back to the electron transport chain and back to PSI, producing ATP only.

items.stem: Describe the role of photosystem II in non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
items.answer: Light absorbed by PSII excites electrons in the chlorophyll a reaction centre to a higher energy level; they are emitted and passed to the electron transport chain; electrons are replaced by photolysis of water, releasing oxygen and protons.
items.markingKey: light excites electrons [1]; passed to ETC [1]; replaced from photolysis [1]; O₂ and H⁺ produced [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain how ATP is made by chemiosmosis in the chloroplast.
items.answer: Energy from electrons in the ETC pumps protons from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen; protons from photolysis add to this; protons diffuse back into the stroma through ATP synthase, driving ADP + Pi → ATP.
items.markingKey: proton pumping into lumen [1]; photolysis adds H⁺ [1]; diffusion through ATP synthase [1]; ATP made [1] [4]

items.stem: Jonas extracted chloroplasts from spinach leaves into ice-cold buffer. Equal volumes of chloroplast suspension and DCPIP solution were placed at different distances from a lamp and the time taken for the blue colour to disappear was recorded. Results table. Distance from the lamp / cm: 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Time for DCPIP to decolourise / s, trial 1: 37, 47, 81, 134, 202, 292; trial 2: 40, 45, 81, 132, 200, 300; trial 3: 38, 44, 80, 130, 199, 309. State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: A line graph: distance from the lamp on the x-axis and mean time for DCPIP to decolourise on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; distance from the lamp on x-axis and time for DCPIP to decolourise on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Lina extracted chloroplasts from spinach leaves into ice-cold buffer. Equal volumes of chloroplast suspension and DCPIP solution were placed at different distances from a lamp and the time taken for the blue colour to disappear was recorded. Results table. Distance from the lamp / cm: 10, 15, 20, 30, 40. Time for DCPIP to decolourise / s, trial 1: 48, 62, 86, 138, 316; trial 2: 50, 65, 82, 140, 212; trial 3: 49, 64, 86, 142, 212. (a) Calculate the mean time for DCPIP to decolourise at 40 cm, ignoring any anomalous result. (b) Describe a suitable control for this investigation and explain why it is needed.
items.answer: (a) 212 s (b) An identical tube wrapped in aluminium foil (kept in the dark): DCPIP should stay blue, showing that light is needed. A tube with boiled chloroplasts shows that functional chloroplasts are required.
items.markingKey: (a) (212 + 212) ÷ 2 [1] = 212 s [1] [2] (b) 1 mark: control described; 1 mark: shows that the change is caused by the independent variable [2]

Equal volumes of chloroplast suspension and DCPIP solution were placed at different distances from a lamp and the time taken for the blue colour to disappear was recorded. Results table. Distance from the lamp / cm: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Time for DCPIP to decolourise / s, trial 1: 56, 93, 157, 258, 379; trial 2: 57, 96, 157, 266, 388; trial 3: 59, 96, 236, 252, 373. (a) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (b) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it.
items.answer: (a) Temperature; volume of chloroplast suspension. (b) Trial 3 at 30 cm (236 s); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated).
items.markingKey: (a) Any two from: temperature; volume of chloroplast suspension; volume and concentration of DCPIP; wavelength / colour of light (same lamp); pH of buffer [2] (b) trial 3 at 30 cm identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2]

items.stem: Chloe extracted chloroplasts from spinach leaves into ice-cold buffer. Equal volumes of chloroplast suspension and DCPIP solution were placed at different distances from a lamp and the time taken for the blue colour to disappear was recorded. Results table. Distance from the lamp / cm: 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Time for DCPIP to decolourise / s, trial 1: 41, 51, 86, 147, 229, 331; trial 2: 42, 53, 87, 145, 226, 499; trial 3: 45, 52, 85, 147, 223, 351. (a) Explain the results. (b) Calculate the relative light intensity, 1/d², at the closest distance tested.
items.answer: (a) Further from the lamp the light intensity is lower (∝ 1/d²), so fewer electrons are excited in the photosystems per second; DCPIP accepts these electrons in place of NADP, so it is reduced more slowly. (b) 0.0400 cm⁻²

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the splitting of water by light energy (at photosystem II) into protons, electrons and oxygen"?
items.answer: Photolysis
items.markingKey: Photolysis: the splitting of water by light energy (at photosystem II) into protons, electrons and oxygen.

items.stem: Which photosystem is involved in cyclic photophosphorylation?
items.answer: Photosystem I only
items.markingKey: Electrons from PSI return via carriers to PSI.

items.stem: Explain why cyclic photophosphorylation is useful to a plant.
items.answer: It provides extra ATP without reduced NADP; the Calvin cycle needs ATP and reduced NADP in a 3:2 ratio, and ATP is needed for other processes such as active transport in guard cells.
items.markingKey: ATP only [1]; extra ATP for Calvin cycle ratio / other processes [1] [2]

items.stem: Compare cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
items.answer: Both: in thylakoid membranes, light excites electrons, ETC and chemiosmosis make ATP. Cyclic: PSI only, electrons return to PSI, no photolysis, no O₂, no reduced NADP. Non-cyclic: PSII and PSI, photolysis, O₂ released, reduced NADP formed.
items.markingKey: similarity [1]; photosystems [1]; photolysis/O₂ [1]; reduced NADP [1] [4]

items.stem: In an experiment in Bangkok, PSII is inhibited by a herbicide. Predict and explain the effect on the products of the light-dependent reactions.
items.answer: Oxygen release and reduced NADP production stop; only cyclic photophosphorylation (ATP) continues.
items.markingKey: O₂ stops [1]; NADP not reduced [1]; cyclic ATP may continue [1] [3]

items.stem: A suspension of isolated chloroplasts in buffer released 80 μmol of oxygen per hour per mg chlorophyll when illuminated with an artificial electron acceptor present, but almost none when the acceptor was absent. (a) Calculate the number of μmol of water split per hour per mg chlorophyll. (b) Calculate the number of μmol of electrons released per hour per mg chlorophyll.
items.answer: (a) 160 μmol (b) 320 μmol

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "RuBP"?
options: The three-carbon sugar formed by reduction of GP; used to make glucose, amino acids and lipids and to regenerate RuBP.
Ribulose bisphosphate: a five-carbon compound that accepts carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle.
Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase: the enzyme that catalyses the fixation of CO₂ by combining it with RuBP.
Glycerate 3-phosphate: the three-carbon compound formed when the unstable six-carbon intermediate splits.
items.answer: Ribulose bisphosphate: a five-carbon compound that accepts carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle.
items.markingKey: RuBP: ribulose bisphosphate: a five-carbon compound that accepts carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle.

items.stem: Explain why the Calvin cycle stops soon after a plant is placed in the dark.
items.answer: In the dark, the light-dependent reactions stop so no ATP or reduced NADP is made; GP cannot be reduced to TP and RuBP cannot be regenerated, so CO₂ fixation stops.
items.markingKey: no ATP / reduced NADP [1]; GP not reduced [1]; RuBP not regenerated [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why the Calvin cycle is described as light-independent although it does not take place for long in the dark.
items.answer: Its reactions do not directly use light; but they depend on a continuous supply of ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent reactions.
items.markingKey: no light used directly [1]; depends on products of LDR [1] [2]

items.stem: Grace supplies a suspension of spinach chloroplasts with radioactive ¹⁴CO₂ and measures the radioactivity in GP and RuBP. Then the temperature is lowered from 25 °C to 5 °C. Predict and explain the changes in GP and RuBP.
items.answer: The rates of all steps fall, so CO₂ fixation slows: Calvin cycle reactions are enzyme-catalysed (e.g. rubisco), so less kinetic energy means fewer enzyme–substrate collisions.
items.markingKey: prediction: the rates of all steps fall, so CO₂ fixation slows [1]; explanation: Calvin cycle reactions are enzyme-catalysed (e.g. rubisco), so less kinetic energy means fewer enzyme–substrate collisions [2] [3]

items.stem: Ethan calculates the requirements of the Calvin cycle. Calculate how many triose phosphate are formed when 6 molecules of CO₂ are fixed in the Calvin cycle. Show your working.
items.markingKey: per CO₂: 3 ATP, 2 reduced NADP, 2 GP, 2 TP (one sixth of TP leaves); 6 turns per hexose. 6 × 2 = 12. Per-CO₂ value [1]; answer [1] [2]

items.stem: In an experiment with a culture of cyanobacteria, the light is switched off. Explain the effect on the Calvin cycle.
items.answer: GP concentration rises and RuBP concentration falls: RuBP still combines with CO₂ to form GP, but GP cannot be reduced (no ATP/reduced NADP) and RuBP is not regenerated.
items.markingKey: prediction: GP concentration rises and RuBP concentration falls [1]; explanation: RuBP still combines with CO₂ to form GP, but GP cannot be reduced (no ATP/reduced NADP) and RuBP is not regenerated [2] [3]

items.stem: In Calvin's "lollipop" experiment, a suspension of Chlorella was illuminated and supplied with ¹⁴CO₂. Samples were run into hot methanol after different times and the labelled compounds separated by two-way chromatography. After 5 s most radioactivity was in GP; after 30 s it was also in triose phosphate, hexose phosphates and RuBP. (a) Explain why GP was the first labelled compound. (b) Explain why two-way chromatography was used.
items.answer: (a) CO₂ is fixed by combining with RuBP (rubisco) to form an unstable 6C compound that immediately splits into two GP. (b) Many compounds with similar Rf values in one solvent are separated better by running in a second solvent at right angles.
items.markingKey: (a) RuBP + CO₂ [1]; forms GP first [1] [2] (b) Many compounds with similar Rf values in one solvent are separated better by running in a second solvent at right angles [2] [2]

items.stem: In Calvin's "lollipop" experiment, a suspension of Chlorella was illuminated and supplied with ¹⁴CO₂. Samples were run into hot methanol after different times and the labelled compounds separated by two-way chromatography. After 5 s most radioactivity was in GP; after 30 s it was also in triose phosphate, hexose phosphates and RuBP. (a) Explain why GP was the first labelled compound. (b) Describe the reduction of GP to triose phosphate.
items.answer: (a) CO₂ is fixed by combining with RuBP (rubisco) to form an unstable 6C compound that immediately splits into two GP. (b) GP is phosphorylated using ATP and reduced using hydrogen from reduced NADP to form triose phosphate; ADP and NADP return to the thylakoids.
items.markingKey: (a) RuBP + CO₂ [1]; forms GP first [1] [2] (b) ATP [1]; reduced NADP [1]; products return [1] [3]

items.stem: Which molecule combines with carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle?
items.answer: Ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP)
items.markingKey: RuBP (5C) + CO₂ → 2 GP, catalysed by rubisco.

items.stem: Which products of the light-dependent reactions are used to reduce GP to triose phosphate?
items.answer: ATP and reduced NADP
items.markingKey: ATP provides energy and reduced NADP provides hydrogen.

items.stem: A suspension of Chlorella is moved from light to darkness. Which change occurs in the first minute?
options: GP concentration rises and RuBP concentration falls
items.answer: GP concentration rises and RuBP concentration falls
items.markingKey: GP no longer reduced; RuBP no longer regenerated.

items.stem: A suspension of spinach chloroplasts is photosynthesising steadily. What happens to the levels of Calvin cycle intermediates when the temperature is lowered from 25 °C to 5 °C?
options: The rates of all steps fall, so CO₂ fixation slows
GP falls slightly and RuBP rises
RuBP concentration rises and GP concentration falls
items.answer: The rates of all steps fall, so CO₂ fixation slows
items.markingKey: The rates of all steps fall, so CO₂ fixation slows: Calvin cycle reactions are enzyme-catalysed (e.g. rubisco), so less kinetic energy means fewer enzyme–substrate collisions.

items.stem: How many turns of the cycle are needed when 18 molecules of CO₂ are fixed in the Calvin cycle?
items.markingKey: per CO₂: 3 ATP, 2 reduced NADP, 2 GP, 2 TP (one sixth of TP leaves); 6 turns per hexose. 18 × 1 = 18.

items.stem: Ravi supplies a culture of cyanobacteria with radioactive ¹⁴CO₂ and measures the radioactivity in GP and RuBP. Then the temperature is lowered from 25 °C to 5 °C. Predict and explain the changes in GP and RuBP.
items.answer: The rates of all steps fall, so CO₂ fixation slows: Calvin cycle reactions are enzyme-catalysed (e.g. rubisco), so less kinetic energy means fewer enzyme–substrate collisions.
items.markingKey: prediction: the rates of all steps fall, so CO₂ fixation slows [1]; explanation: Calvin cycle reactions are enzyme-catalysed (e.g. rubisco), so less kinetic energy means fewer enzyme–substrate collisions [2] [3]

items.stem: What is the name for "the deliberate raising of CO₂ concentration, temperature and light in a glasshouse to remove limiting factors and increase yield"?
items.answer: Glasshouse enrichment
items.markingKey: Glasshouse enrichment: the deliberate raising of CO₂ concentration, temperature and light in a glasshouse to remove limiting factors and increase yield.

items.stem: Explain why increasing the temperature from 15 °C to 25 °C may have no effect on the rate of photosynthesis at low light intensity.
items.answer: At low light intensity, light is the limiting factor; temperature affects only the enzyme-catalysed Calvin cycle, which is already limited by the supply of ATP and reduced NADP.
items.markingKey: light limiting [1]; temperature affects Calvin cycle enzymes not light-dependent reactions [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how growers can use their knowledge of limiting factors to increase crop yields in glasshouses.
items.answer: Raise CO₂ (paraffin burners/CO₂ cylinders), supplementary lighting at suitable wavelengths and heating to optimum; each is raised until another factor limits; balance cost against extra yield.
items.markingKey: CO₂ [1]; light [1]; temperature [1]; cost-effectiveness / another factor limits [1] [4]

items.stem: Priya placed a piece of Elodea in 0.5% sodium hydrogencarbonate solution at 25 °C and counted the bubbles released per minute with a lamp at different distances. Results table. Distance from the lamp / cm: 8, 12, 16, 20, 30, 40. Number of bubbles per minute, trial 1: 52, 47, 33, 26, 13, 8; trial 2: 52, 46, 33, 27, 13, 8; trial 3: 55, 44, 36, 25, 13, 8. Calculate the mean number of bubbles per minute at 40 cm.

Priya placed a piece of Elodea in 0.5% sodium hydrogencarbonate solution at 25 °C and counted the bubbles released per minute with a lamp at different distances. Results table. Distance from the lamp / cm: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. Number of bubbles per minute, trial 1: 56, 53, 39, 28, 19, 21; trial 2: 58, 51, 40, 27, 19, 15; trial 3: 58, 55, 40, 28, 19, 14. (a) Describe the trend shown by the results. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) As the distance from the lamp increases, the number of bubbles per minute decreases and then levels off at about 25 cm. (b) Collect the gas in a photosynthometer and measure the volume.

items.stem: On a graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity, the curves at 0.04% and 0.1% CO₂ are identical at low light. Why?
options: Carbon dioxide is limiting at low light
Photosynthesis does not occur at low light
Temperature is limiting at low light
Light intensity is the limiting factor at low intensities
items.answer: Light intensity is the limiting factor at low intensities
items.markingKey: CO₂ has no effect while light limits.

items.stem: Explain why counting bubbles is not an accurate method of measuring the rate of photosynthesis.
items.answer: Bubbles vary in size; some oxygen dissolves in the water or is used in respiration; gas may contain other gases; bubbles hard to count at high rates.
items.markingKey: bubble size varies [1]; another valid reason [1] [2]

items.stem: A graph shows the rate of photosynthesis of a crop plant against light intensity under three conditions: A — 0.02% CO₂ at 10 °C (levels off at 24 units); B — 0.15% CO₂ at 10 °C (levels off at 35 units); C — 0.15% CO₂ at 20 °C (levels off at 55 units). At low light intensities the three curves are identical. Explain why increasing temperature increases the rate only at high light intensity.
items.answer: Temperature affects the enzyme-controlled Calvin cycle (e.g. rubisco); at low light the supply of ATP/reduced NADP limits the rate instead.
items.markingKey: enzymes of Calvin cycle [1]; light limits at low intensity [1] [2]

items.stem: Mohammed placed a piece of Elodea in 0.5% sodium hydrogencarbonate solution at 25 °C and counted the bubbles released per minute with a lamp at different distances. Results table. Distance from the lamp / cm: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Number of bubbles per minute, trial 1: 58, 30, 16, 14, 6; trial 2: 60, 31, 16, 9, 6; trial 3: 60, 29, 16, 10, 6. (a) Explain the results. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (c) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) Closer to the lamp the light intensity is higher (∝ 1/d²), so more light energy is absorbed and the light-dependent reactions are faster, producing more oxygen; at the closest distances another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature limits the rate, so it levels off. (b) Collect the gas in a photosynthometer and measure the volume. (c) A line graph: distance from the lamp on the x-axis and mean number of bubbles per minute on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) light intensity and distance [1]; faster LDR / more O₂ [1]; another factor limits at high intensity [1] [3] (b) Any one from: collect the gas in a photosynthometer and measure the volume; place a heat filter (beaker of water) between lamp and plant; allow 5 minutes acclimatisation at each distance; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the distance from the lamp (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (c) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; distance from the lamp on x-axis and number of bubbles per minute on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Which colours of light are absorbed most strongly by chlorophyll a?
items.answer: Blue and red
items.markingKey: Peaks near 430 nm and 660 nm; green is reflected.

items.stem: Explain how the thylakoid membranes are adapted for the light-dependent reactions.
items.answer: Large surface area in grana for many photosystems; contain pigments arranged in photosystems, electron carriers and ATP synthase; enclose a small lumen for building a proton gradient.
items.markingKey: surface area [1]; photosystems / carriers / ATP synthase [1]; lumen for proton gradient [1] [3]

items.stem: Ana separated the pigments in a leaf extract by thin-layer chromatography. The solvent front moved 10.6 cm. Three spots were seen: spot A (orange-yellow) 10.2 cm, spot B (grey) 8.8 cm, spot C (yellow) 7.4 cm from the origin. Published Rf values for this solvent are: carotene: 0.95; phaeophytin: 0.81; xanthophyll: 0.71; chlorophyll a: 0.65; chlorophyll b: 0.45. Explain why the origin line is drawn in pencil and kept above the level of the solvent.
items.answer: Pencil (graphite) does not dissolve and run in the solvent; if the origin were below the solvent the pigments would dissolve into the solvent in the beaker.
items.markingKey: pencil insoluble [1]; pigments would dissolve into solvent [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the structure of a chloroplast and explain how it is adapted for photosynthesis.
items.answer: Double envelope; thylakoids stacked into grana joined by intergranal lamellae; photosystems, electron carriers and ATP synthase in thylakoid membranes; lumen for proton gradient; stroma with Calvin cycle enzymes (rubisco), starch grains, lipid droplets, 70S ribosomes, circular DNA.
items.markingKey: envelope [1]; grana / thylakoids and surface area [2]; photosystems and pigments [1]; lumen [1]; stroma enzymes [1]; DNA/ribosomes [1] [7]

items.stem: What is the source of the oxygen released in photosynthesis?
items.answer: Water
items.markingKey: Photolysis: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂.

items.stem: Sofia writes in a revision note: "Light energy is used directly to make glucose in the light-dependent reactions." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Light energy is used to make ATP and reduced NADP; carbohydrate is made in the Calvin cycle using these products.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Light energy is used to make ATP and reduced NADP; carbohydrate is made in the Calvin cycle using these products. [2]

items.stem: Diego says: "The oxygen released by plants comes from carbon dioxide." Explain whether Diego is correct.
items.answer: The oxygen comes from the photolysis of water at photosystem II; the oxygen in CO₂ ends up in carbohydrate and water.

items.stem: Tomás predicts the effect on the light-dependent reactions when chloroplasts are illuminated with only light of wavelength 700 nm. Explain what Tomás should predict.

items.stem: A suspension of isolated chloroplasts in buffer released 30 μmol of oxygen per hour per mg chlorophyll when illuminated with an artificial electron acceptor present, but almost none when the acceptor was absent. (a) Calculate the number of μmol of water split per hour per mg chlorophyll. (b) Describe the route of electrons from water to NADP.
items.answer: (a) 60 μmol (b) Water → PSII (excited by light) → electron transport chain → PSI (re-excited) → ferredoxin/NADP reductase → NADP.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "ribulose bisphosphate: a five-carbon compound that accepts carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle"?
items.answer: RuBP
items.markingKey: RuBP: ribulose bisphosphate: a five-carbon compound that accepts carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle.

items.stem: Describe the three main stages of the Calvin cycle.
items.answer: Fixation: CO₂ + RuBP → 2 GP (rubisco); reduction: GP → TP using ATP and reduced NADP; regeneration: most TP converted to RuBP using ATP.
items.markingKey: fixation [1]; reduction [1]; regeneration [1] [3]

items.stem: In an experiment with a culture of cyanobacteria, the temperature is lowered from 25 °C to 5 °C. Explain the effect on the Calvin cycle.
items.answer: The rates of all steps fall, so CO₂ fixation slows: Calvin cycle reactions are enzyme-catalysed (e.g. rubisco), so less kinetic energy means fewer enzyme–substrate collisions.
items.markingKey: prediction: the rates of all steps fall, so CO₂ fixation slows [1]; explanation: Calvin cycle reactions are enzyme-catalysed (e.g. rubisco), so less kinetic energy means fewer enzyme–substrate collisions [2] [3]

items.stem: How many reduced NADP are used when 1 molecule of CO₂ is fixed in the Calvin cycle?
items.markingKey: per CO₂: 3 ATP, 2 reduced NADP, 2 GP, 2 TP (one sixth of TP leaves); 6 turns per hexose. 1 × 2 = 2.

items.stem: Isla calculates the requirements of the Calvin cycle. Calculate how many molecules of hexose are formed when 12 molecules of CO₂ are fixed in the Calvin cycle. Show your working.

items.stem: In Calvin's "lollipop" experiment, a suspension of Chlorella was illuminated and supplied with ¹⁴CO₂. Samples were run into hot methanol after different times and the labelled compounds separated by two-way chromatography. After 5 s most radioactivity was in GP; after 30 s it was also in triose phosphate, hexose phosphates and RuBP. (a) Explain why the samples were run into hot methanol. (b) Explain why GP was the first labelled compound. (c) Explain why radioactivity later appeared in RuBP.
items.answer: (a) Hot methanol kills the cells and denatures the enzymes instantly, stopping the reactions at a known time. (b) CO₂ is fixed by combining with RuBP (rubisco) to form an unstable 6C compound that immediately splits into two GP. (c) Labelled triose phosphate is used to regenerate RuBP, so the label passes into RuBP.
items.markingKey: (a) kills / denatures enzymes [1]; stops reactions at exact time [1] [2] (b) RuBP + CO₂ [1]; forms GP first [1] [2] (c) TP regenerates RuBP [1]; label carried [1] [2]

items.answer: Some of the oxygen produced is used in respiration by the plant, so the oxygen released is net (apparent) photosynthesis.
